title: THE SECOND COMING OF CHRIST
summary: MEMORY VERSE: Matthew 24:44 — "Therefore you also be ready, for the son of man is coming at an hour you do not expect."
body:
## **LESSON GUIDELINES**

# The Climax of Christ's Sermon (24:27-28, 30-31, 40-41): The Second Coming

# 1. The Signal (24:30)

The Son of Man will appear in the heavens.

# 2. The Swiftness (24:27)

As the lightning flashes across the sky.

# 3. The Summons (24:31)

Angels will be sent forth with a mighty trumpet blast to gather the people of Israel from the farthest ends of the earth and heaven.

# 4. The Slaughter (24:28, 40-41): Armageddon!

## a. The Assembling of the Victims (24:40-41)

One will be taken, another left.

## b. The Appearing of the Vultures (24:28)

To eat the bodies of the slain warriors!

# The Clue to Christ's Sermon (24:32-35): The Rebirth of Israel

## A. The Parable (24:32)

A sprouting fig tree.

## B. The Prophecy (24:33-34)

# i. The When (24:33)

# ii. The Who (24:34)

## C. The Permanence (24:35)

Heaven and earth will pass away, but His word is eternal.

## **SUMMARY**

Christ's coming at an unknown time is to be as unexpected as the coming of a thief who breaks into a house. Thus the devoted disciple must be ready at anytime for the Lord's appearance. Once again, Christ refers to His return for the faithful of His churches at an unexpected and unknown time.

1. This warning is not for tribulation saints. The only way to harmonize Christ's teaching about His unexpected coming with His statement concerning His expected coming is to assume two phases to His second coming. The first stage involves Christ's return at an unexpected time to take believers from earth (1 Thessalonians 4:17; Revelation 3:10) and the second stage is His coming at the end of the age at an expected time — after the tribulation and cosmic signs (Matthew 24:29-30) — to destroy the wicked and begin His reign on earth (Revelation 19:11-21; 20:4).

2. This second coming of Christ as one event consisting of two phases parallels Christ's coming predicted in the Old Testament — which speaks of one coming of the Messiah but sees its fulfilment in two phases: His coming to die for sin and His coming to reign (9:2-7; 40:3-5); compare Isaiah 61:1-3 with Luke 4:18-19; 9:7.

3. Christ's urgent warning to be always spiritually ready for His unexpected coming — the Rapture — applies to all generations of Christians before the tribulation. It is a motive for perseverance in the faith.

#References: 
**John 14:3; Isaiah 9:7.**
discussion_questions:
Why does Jesus use the image of a thief in the night to describe His coming — and what specific aspect of readiness does this image demand from the believer?

How does the two-phase model of the second coming resolve the apparent contradiction between Jesus' teaching about His unexpected coming and His teaching about visible signs that precede it?

The fig tree parable connects the rebirth of Israel to the nearness of the end — what does it mean theologically and practically that the fulfilment of this sign has occurred within living memory?

Jesus says heaven and earth will pass away but His words will not — how does the eternal reliability of His word function as the foundation for all end-times confidence?

The summons of angels with a trumpet blast will gather the elect from the farthest ends of creation — what does this cosmic gathering communicate about God's attention to every individual believer?

Armageddon assembles the armies of the nations against Christ and they are destroyed — how does this final battle reframe the apparent victories of the antichrist throughout the tribulation period?

Christ's urgent call to readiness applies to all generations of Christians — what does it mean for a believer in a relatively calm season to live with genuine eschatological urgency?

How does the two-phase second coming parallel the two-phase first coming — and what does this pattern reveal about God's way of fulfilling prophecy?

The believer who is taken at the Rapture and the believer who endures through the tribulation both arrive at the same destination — what does this say about the different paths God may lead His people through in the last days?

If readiness for Christ's return is the motive for perseverance — what specific area of your life does that readiness most urgently need to reshape right now?

analysis:
## BACKGROUND & CONTEXT

Matthew 24 reaches its climax in verses 27-44 — the most concentrated prophetic teaching Jesus ever delivered in a single sitting. Having described the signs of the end, the Great Tribulation, and the cosmic disturbances that will precede His return, Jesus now turns to the nature of His coming itself: its visibility, its swiftness, its summons of the elect, and its devastating judgment of the wicked. He then grounds this teaching in a parable — the fig tree — and closes with one of His most urgent pastoral commands: be ready.

The lesson covers two related but distinct aspects of Christ's return: the visible, glorious coming at the end of the tribulation, and the unexpected, sudden coming before it — the Rapture — which takes believers from the earth prior to the tribulation's most severe phase. Understanding both phases is essential for a coherent theology of the last days.

## SUMMARY & APPLICATION

# The Fig Tree — Israel and the Nearness of the End (Matthew 24:32-34)

Jesus uses the fig tree as a parable of discernment: when its branch becomes tender and puts forth leaves, you know that summer is near. So also, when you see all these things, know that it is near — at the doors. The fig tree in prophetic imagery is consistently associated with Israel. The rebirth of Israel as a nation — an event that has occurred within living memory — is understood by many expositors as the budding of the fig tree that Jesus described. The generation that witnesses this budding will also witness the fulfilment of all these things.

The permanence statement of verse 35 grounds the entire prophetic programme in the reliability of Jesus' word: heaven and earth will pass away, but My words will by no means pass away. Every specific sign, every prophetic detail, every timeline Jesus announced in Matthew 24 is backed by the most durable guarantee in existence — the eternal word of the Son of God.

# The Signal and the Swiftness — Visible and Sudden (Matthew 24:27, 30)

The second coming of Christ will be neither invisible nor secret in its final phase. Verse 27 compares it to lightning that flashes from east to west — instantaneous, simultaneous, universally visible. There will be no ambiguity about whether it has happened. Verse 30 adds that all the tribes of the earth will mourn when they see the Son of Man coming on the clouds of heaven with power and great glory. The coming that ends the tribulation is the most spectacular event in all of human history.

This visible coming stands in contrast to the unexpected, thief-like coming of the Rapture — which takes believers before the tribulation at an hour no one knows. The two phases together answer what appears to be a contradiction in Jesus' teaching: He warns both that His coming will be unexpected and that it will be preceded by visible signs. The resolution is two phases: unexpected first phase, sign-preceded second phase.

# The Summons — Angels, Trumpets, and Gathered Elect (Matthew 24:31)

At the visible return, angels will be sent with a great sound of a trumpet to gather together His elect from the four winds, from one end of heaven to the other. This cosmic gathering is the reunion of God's people — scattered across every corner of creation — into the presence of their returning King. No believer will be missed. No one will be left in a remote location too far for the angel's reach. The trumpet blast will be heard at the farthest ends of the earth and heaven.

This summons completes the arc that Daniel 7 began: the saints who suffered under the beast, who endured the tribulation, who refused the mark — they will be gathered to possess the kingdom that the Son of Man receives from the Ancient of Days. The suffering was real. The gathering will be more real.

# Armageddon — The Assembling and the Slaughter (Matthew 24:28, 40-41)

The appearance of vultures gathering over a carcass — verse 28 — is an image of Armageddon: the final battle in which the armies of the nations assemble against Christ and are destroyed. One will be taken and another left — not a description of the Rapture in this context, but of the separation that Armageddon produces: the wicked gathered for judgment, the righteous preserved. The slain warriors of Armageddon are not God's people — they are the armies that assembled against the Lamb and were overcome by the word of His mouth.

Revelation 19:19-20 fills in the detail: the beast, the kings of the earth, and their armies assembled to make war against the rider on the white horse and His army — and the beast was captured and thrown alive into the lake of fire. Armageddon is not the defeat of the saints. It is the defeat of everything that has ever stood against them.

# Two Phases — One Coming (Summary Point 1-2)

The summary of this lesson resolves the apparent tension in Jesus' teaching by proposing what many expositors hold as the two-phase model of the second coming. The first phase — unexpected, thief-like, pre-tribulation — is the Rapture: Christ returns in the air to take believers from the earth before the tribulation begins (1 Thessalonians 4:17; Revelation 3:10). The second phase — expected, sign-preceded, post-tribulation — is the visible return in glory to destroy the wicked and establish His reign on earth.

This two-phase model parallels the Old Testament prophecies of the Messiah — which spoke of one coming but saw its fulfilment in two: the first coming to die for sin, and the second coming to reign. The same hermeneutical pattern applies to the second coming itself.

# Readiness as the Posture of Every Generation (Summary Point 3)

Christ's warning to be ready is not addressed only to the generation that will experience the tribulation. It applies to all generations of Christians before the tribulation. Every believer in every age lives in the light of an imminent return — a return that could come before this generation passes. This posture of readiness is not anxiety — it is the motive for perseverance. The believer who keeps the return in view will not grow complacent, will not make peace with the spirit of the age, and will not invest their life in things that the coming King will burn away.

## FURTHER APPLICATION

**Learn to read the signs** — The fig tree parable is a call to discernment. Study the prophetic programme of Scripture well enough to recognise what season you are in — and let that recognition produce urgency rather than complacency.

**Live in two-phase awareness** — Understand both the unexpected Rapture and the visible return. Do not collapse them into one event or separate them so far that neither shapes your daily living. Both are real, both are coming, and both demand a response now.

**Be ready before the moment comes** — Jesus does not call the disciples to get ready when the signs appear — He calls them to already be ready. The spiritual preparation required for the return of Christ is not a last-minute exercise. It is the work of a daily, sustained, faithful life.

**Let the return reorder your priorities** — Heaven and earth will pass away. Every investment, every ambition, every accumulation that is oriented toward this age alone will pass with it. Invest in what is eternal — the Word, the kingdom, the souls of people — because these will remain when everything else is shaken.

**Use the return as a motive for perseverance** — When the faith becomes costly, when the world's pressure to conform intensifies, when endurance is the only option left — remember that the One who is coming is coming soon. The posture of the returning King's servant is not collapse but faithful continuance.
analysis_points:
The second coming of Christ is not a vague theological concept — it is a specific, visible, cosmic event that every eye will see.

Readiness for Christ's return is not a one-time decision — it is a sustained posture of spiritual alertness maintained across an entire lifetime.

The fig tree parable is not merely agricultural — it is a prophetic signal about the rebirth of Israel and the nearness of the end.

Heaven and earth will pass away, but the Word of God is eternal — the prophetic programme announced in Scripture will be fulfilled without exception.

The second coming operates in two phases — the unexpected rapture for the faithful before the tribulation, and the visible return in glory at its conclusion.

Christ's urgent call to readiness applies to all generations of believers — not only to those living in the final days.

The summons of angels at the trumpet blast will gather God's people from the farthest ends of creation — no believer will be left behind or overlooked.

Armageddon is not the defeat of God's people — it is the defeat of every force that has assembled against God's anointed.

The warning to be ready functions as a motive for perseverance — the believer who keeps the return in view will not grow complacent.

Christ's coming is compared to a thief in the night — not because it will be secret, but because it will be sudden and without warning for those who are not watching.

title: BEWARE OF THE MARK OF THE BEAST

## LESSON GUIDELINES

John sees two beasts, one from the sea and one from the earth, symbolizing the Antichrist and his false prophets.

# 1. The Beast Out of the Sea (Revelation 13:1-18): This is the Antichrist

## a. His Appearance (13:1-2)

# i. He has ten horns (each with a crown) and seven heads (each with a blasphemous name) (13:1)

# ii. He looks like a leopard with feet like a bear and a mouth like a lion (13:2a)

## b. His Authority (13:2b)

It comes from satan himself.

## c. His (Possible) Assassination (13:3a)

Some believe he will be killed and then rise from the dead.

## d. His Adulation (13:3b-4, 8)

Following this, the entire world is astonished and worships him.

## e. His Arrogance (13:5-6)

For a period of forty-two months, he blasphemes God.

## f. His Activities (13:7, 9-10)

# i. In Regard to God's People (13:7a, 9-10)

The cruelty (13:7a, 9-10a): he persecutes and conquers them.

The challenge (13:10b): they are exhorted to display endurance and faithfulness.

# ii. In Regard to All People (13:7b)

He rules over them.

## a. His Mission (13:11-12)

With the appearance of a lamb but the voice of a dragon, he forces the world to worship the Antichrist.

## b. His Miracles (13:13, 15)

He performs great miracles.

# i. He calls down fire from heaven (13:13)

# ii. He gives life to a statue (13:14-15)

This statue bears the image of the Antichrist.

## c. His Mark (13:16-18)

# i. What is it (13:18)

It is the number 666.

# ii. Where it is applied (13:16)

Either on the right hand or forehead.

# iii. Why it is applied (13:17)

No one is able to buy, sell, etc without it.

## SUMMARY

A decree will be given to kill all who refuse to worship the world ruler and his images. In other words, many who resist the antichrist and remain faithful and loyal to Jesus will pay with their lives. The antichrist will seek to gain total economic control of the world. All people must worship him and receive a mark on their hands or foreheads in order to buy or sell. This economic pressure will help identify the followers of the world religion promoted by the antichrist. Those who refuse to take the mark will be hunted down in order to be killed. Although the antichrist is called "the beast" throughout Revelation, his number is 666. Many commentators believe that six is the number for humanity in Scripture and three is the number for God. Therefore, the three sixes could very well refer to a man who makes himself god. Like the Roman emperors and many both before and after them, he believes he is a god (2 Thessalonians 2:4).

**References:** *Revelation 14:12-13.*
discussion_questions:
Why does the antichrist's authority come specifically from satan — and what does this reveal about the true nature of all anti-God political power throughout history?

The antichrist's possible death and resurrection appears to be a deliberate counterfeit of Christ's resurrection — what does this tell us about the enemy's deepest strategy in the last days?

The false prophet has the appearance of a lamb but speaks like a dragon — in what ways is religious deception more dangerous than open hostility to the faith?

The forty-two months of the antichrist's dominion are a fixed, God-determined period — how does knowing that the tribulation has a divine boundary change the posture of the believer who faces it?

The mark of the beast is primarily an economic control system — how does this specific form of persecution differ from physical violence, and why might it be more effective at identifying genuine believers?

The number 666 represents a man making himself God — in what ways is the spirit of the antichrist already visible in contemporary culture's elevation of human autonomy above divine authority?

Revelation 13:10 calls for endurance and faithfulness rather than resistance — what does this tell us about the primary spiritual virtue required for last-days living?

How does a believer practically prepare themselves now — theologically, spiritually, and practically — for the economic exclusion that refusing the mark will produce?

The entire world worships the antichrist — how does a believer maintain their distinctiveness and resist universal social pressure when the majority have aligned with the beast?

Revelation 14:12-13 calls those who die refusing the mark "blessed" — how does a theology of blessing that includes martyrdom reshape the believer's understanding of what it means to win?

analysis:
## BACKGROUND & CONTEXT

Revelation 13 is one of the most studied and debated chapters in all of Scripture — and also one of the most practically important for the last-days believer. It presents a detailed portrait of the two central figures of the tribulation period: the antichrist, rising from the sea with universal political and military authority, and the false prophet, rising from the earth with religious and economic authority. Together they form a satanic trinity — a counterfeit of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit — designed to draw the worship of the entire world away from the living God.

The chapter is not written to terrify the believer. It is written to prepare them. John's vision gives the church a detailed advance knowledge of what the last days' persecution will look like — so that when it comes, those who have read and understood will not be surprised, deceived, or unprepared.

## SUMMARY & APPLICATION

# The Beast From the Sea — The Antichrist (Revelation 13:1-10)

The beast from the sea combines the characteristics of the four beasts of Daniel 7 — the leopard, the bear, the lion, and the unnamed fourth — into a single figure. He is the culmination and concentration of every beastly empire that has preceded him. His ten horns with crowns represent political authority over ten kingdoms. His seven heads with blasphemous names represent his comprehensive assault on the knowledge and worship of God.

His authority comes not from human election or military conquest alone — it comes from the dragon, which is satan. Revelation 13:2b makes this explicit: the dragon gave him his power, his throne, and great authority. The antichrist is not simply a gifted politician or a brilliant military strategist. He is the human instrument of satan's final, most concentrated bid for global worship.

The possible assassination and resurrection of the antichrist — one of his heads appears to have received a fatal wound, and yet the wound was healed — is designed to counterfeit the death and resurrection of Jesus Christ. The world's astonished worship follows precisely from this apparent miracle. The enemy's deepest strategy is not to deny the resurrection but to imitate it.

# The Forty-Two Months — A Fixed and Bounded Season (Revelation 13:5-6)

The antichrist is given authority for forty-two months — three and a half years. This is the same period referenced in Daniel 7, Matthew 24, and Revelation 11 and 12. The repetition of this specific duration across multiple prophetic passages is significant: it communicates that the most severe period of tribulation is not open-ended. God has set a boundary on the beast's season of dominion. The blasphemy will be permitted. The persecution will be allowed. But the clock is already running — and when the forty-two months are complete, the court will be seated and the beast will be destroyed.

For the believer enduring the antichrist's persecution, this is not a small comfort — it is a foundational one. The tribulation has a fixed end-date known to God. The endurance called for in verse 10 is not endurance without a horizon. It is endurance within a period that God has already measured and bounded.

# The False Prophet — Religion in the Service of the Beast (Revelation 13:11-15)

The beast from the earth — identified elsewhere in Revelation as the false prophet — is in many ways more dangerous than the antichrist himself. He has the appearance of a lamb — religious, gentle, approachable — but speaks with the voice of a dragon. He is the antichrist's propaganda minister, his religious public relations machine, his miracle-working enforcer.

His miracles are specifically designed to manufacture worship: he calls fire from heaven — counterfeiting Elijah — and gives life to the image of the antichrist, causing it to speak. These signs are not the miracles of the kingdom of God. They are the signs of the kingdom of deception. Jesus warned in Matthew 24 that false prophets would show great signs and wonders, so as to deceive, if possible, even the elect. The false prophet of Revelation 13 is the ultimate expression of this warning. Miracles are not, in themselves, proof of divine origin — they must be tested against the Word of God.

# The Mark — Economic Control as Religious Persecution (Revelation 13:16-18)

The mark of the beast is the antichrist's final instrument of total control. It is required for all — small and great, rich and poor, free and slave — on their right hand or forehead. Without it, no one can buy or sell. The economic dimension of the mark is its primary enforcement mechanism. The antichrist does not need to station soldiers at every door — he simply controls the global economy. Without the mark, the faithful cannot purchase food, pay rent, conduct business, or participate in any commercial transaction.

This is the choice the tribulation believer will face in its starkest form: receive the mark and survive economically, or refuse the mark and face economic exclusion, persecution, and ultimately execution. The number 666 — the number of the beast — represents humanity's ultimate attempt to be God. Six is the number of man; three is the number of God. Three sixes is man aspiring to divine status — the antichrist who sits in the temple declaring himself to be God, as 2 Thessalonians 2:4 describes.

Revelation 14:12-13 — referenced in this lesson — provides the answer for those who face this choice: here is the patience of the saints, those who keep the commandments of God and the faith of Jesus. And John hears a voice from heaven: blessed are the dead who die in the Lord from now on. The faithful who refuse the mark and pay with their lives are not losers in God's economy — they are blessed.

## FURTHER APPLICATION

**Guard against false miracles** — The last days will be saturated with signs and wonders. Not all of them will be from God. Build your discernment on the Word, not on the spectacular, and test every sign against the testimony of Scripture.

**Prepare theologically for economic pressure** — The mark of the beast uses economic exclusion as its primary tool. Begin now to build a theology of suffering and self-denial that will sustain you when faithfulness to Christ becomes commercially costly.

**Count the cost before the crisis** — The tribulation believer who has not already decided what they will not do for economic security will be far more vulnerable to the mark than one who has already settled the question in advance. Decide now what your line is.

**Understand endurance as the specific calling** — Revelation 13:10 does not call the saints to military resistance. It calls them to endurance and faithfulness. The weapon of the last-days believer against the beast is not the sword — it is the steadfast refusal to bow.

**Find comfort in the fixed boundary** — The forty-two months are not a guess or an estimate. They are a divine appointment — a period that God has measured, bounded, and already marked for conclusion. The beast's season is temporary. The kingdom of God is eternal.
analysis_points:
The antichrist does not rise in a vacuum — his authority comes directly from satan, not from human institutions alone.

The mark of the beast is not merely a religious symbol — it is an economic control system designed to make faithfulness to Christ commercially impossible.

The number 666 is not a random code — it is the number of a man who makes himself God, the ultimate expression of human pride taken to its final conclusion.

Those who refuse the mark will be hunted to be killed — faithfulness in the last days will carry a literal cost that must be counted in advance.

The false prophet's miracles are designed to manufacture worship, not to demonstrate truth — signs and wonders in the last days must be tested against the Word.

The beast from the sea and the beast from the earth work together — the antichrist requires a religious propaganda machine to sustain his global dominion.

Economic pressure will be the primary tool used to identify and eliminate the followers of Christ in the tribulation period.

The entire world will be astonished and will worship the antichrist — the pressure to conform will be universal, not localised.

Endurance and faithfulness are the specific virtues called for in the face of the beast's persecution — not military resistance but spiritual steadfastness.

The antichrist's forty-two months of blasphemy are a fixed, God-determined period — even the beast operates within the boundaries God has set.

## LESSON GUIDELINES

During the first and third years of Belshazzar's reign in Babylon, Daniel has two visions of future Gentiles world powers.

# 1. The First Vision (Daniel 7:1-28): During the First Year of Belshazzar's Reign

## A. The Information (7:1-14): Daniel Sees:

# i. A Lionlike Beast (7:1-4)

"As I watched, its wings were pulled off, and it was left standing with its two hind feet on the ground, like a human being. And a human mind was given to it."

# ii. A Bearlike Beast (Daniel 7:5)

It holds three ribs between its teeth.

# iii. A Leopardlike Beast (7:6)

It has four birds' wings on its back and four heads and is given great authority.

# iv. A 10-Horned Beast (7:7-8)

It is by far the most dreadful and terrifying creature yet. An 11th horn grows, yanking out 3 of the 10 horns.

# v. The Ancient One (7:9-12)

## a. Who is it (7:9)

God Himself is seated in all His heavenly glory, preparing to judge the world.

## b. What Happens (7:10-12)

A river of fire flows from God's presence (7:10a).

Millions of angels minister to Him (7:10b).

Tens of millions of people await judgment (7:10c).

The fourth beast is thrown into hell (7:11-12).

## SUMMARY

Some modern writers take these beasts to represent nations existing in the end times. Most Bible expositors, however, take this vision to parallel Nebuchadnezzar's dream in Daniel 2:37-43, noting but to reveal the bestial, i.e., the inner characteristics of the kingdoms.

1. The lion, a symbol of royal power, represents the Neo-Babylonian Empire. The eagle, the king of birds, may specially represent King Nebuchadnezzar's power, and the plucking of the wings represents what happened in Daniel 4.

2. The bear raised up on one side represents Medo-Persia, with Persia dominating Media. The three ribs in its mouth may represent its conquests of Babylon, Lydia and Egypt.

3. The leopard, a powerful and swift animal, with its four wings, represents Alexander's Greek empire and his rapid conquests. The four heads are the four kingdoms that came out of his empire when he died, for it was divided among his generals; Lysimachus (who took Thrace and Bithynia), Cassander (who took Greece and Macedonia), Seleucus (who took Babylonia and Syria) and Ptolemy (who took the Holy Land, Egypt and Arabia).

4. The fourth beast, dreadful and terrible, and with iron teeth, represents Rome, as does the reminder of the image, including the ten toes. The little horn symbolizes the last great ruler in the world — the antichrist, the man of sin, the beast who puts down three of the ten kings. He will make war with God's saints, overpower them and speak words against God. When Jesus Christ comes, the saints will possess the kingdom, the antichrist will be destroyed and consigned to the lake of fire.

#References: 
**2 Thessalonians 2:3,8; 1 John 2:18; Revelation 13:7; 19:19-20; 11:15-18; 20:4-6; 19:20.**
discussion_questions:
Why does God choose the imagery of beasts to describe world empires — what does this reveal about how heaven evaluates earthly power?

What does the progression from lion to bear to leopard to the unnamed fourth beast communicate about the trajectory of human civilisation apart from God?

The plucking of the lion's wings refers to Nebuchadnezzar's humiliation — what does this say about God's willingness to break even the greatest earthly power to produce repentance?

Most Bible expositors connect the four beasts to Babylon, Medo-Persia, Greece, and Rome — how does this historical fulfilment strengthen confidence in the parts of the vision that are still future?

The little horn wars against God's saints and overpowers them — how does the believer reconcile this with a theology of God's protection and sovereignty?

What does the scene of the Ancient of Days seated in heavenly court communicate about God's relationship to human history — and how does it reframe the apparent victories of the beast?

The Son of Man receives an everlasting kingdom from the Ancient of Days — how does this image in Daniel 7 connect to Jesus' own use of the title "Son of Man" in the Gospels?

The saints of the Most High are promised the eternal kingdom — what does it mean to live as a recipient of that kingdom in a world still dominated by beastly powers?

How does the certainty of the antichrist's destruction and consignment to the lake of fire function as pastoral comfort for believers facing tribulation?

If Daniel 7 ends with the saints possessing the kingdom forever and ever — what difference should that ending make to how you face the most difficult aspects of your present season?

analysis:
## BACKGROUND & CONTEXT

Daniel 7 stands as one of the most significant prophetic passages in all of Scripture. Written during the reign of Belshazzar — the last Babylonian king before the Medo-Persian conquest — it gives Daniel a vision that spans the entire arc of Gentile world dominion from his own day to the end of time. Where Daniel 2 showed these same empires through the image of a great statue — emphasising their outward magnificence — Daniel 7 reveals their inner character through the imagery of beasts. The contrast is intentional and profound: what man sees as glorious civilisation, God sees as predatory, destructive, and ultimately temporary.

The vision does not end with the beasts. It ends with the Ancient of Days seated in judgment, the fourth beast destroyed, and the Son of Man receiving an everlasting kingdom. This is the interpretive key to the entire passage: the beasts rise and fall, but the kingdom of God stands forever.

## SUMMARY & APPLICATION

# The Lion — Neo-Babylonian Empire (7:1-4)

The lion with eagle's wings is the first beast — representing Babylon, the greatest empire of Daniel's day. The eagle's wings speak of the swift, soaring power of Nebuchadnezzar's conquests. But the wings are plucked — a reference to the humiliation of Nebuchadnezzar in Daniel 4, when God stripped him of his power and drove him to live like an animal until he acknowledged that the Most High rules in the kingdoms of men. The beast is left standing like a human, with a human mind given to it — a picture of restored sanity and, ultimately, of the limits of even the mightiest earthly empire. Babylon fell not because of military weakness but because God had set the time of its dominion.

# The Bear — Medo-Persian Empire (7:5)

The bear, raised up on one side with three ribs in its teeth, represents Medo-Persia — the empire that conquered Babylon, Lydia, and Egypt. Persia dominated Media, just as the one raised side of the bear indicates. The three ribs in its teeth are the conquered nations held between the jaws of Persian power. The bear is a heavier, slower animal than the lion — Medo-Persia was a more bureaucratic, less culturally brilliant empire than Babylon, but it was vast and powerful. It too would fall.

# The Leopard — Greek Empire of Alexander (7:6)

The leopard with four wings represents the Greek empire of Alexander the Great — one of history's most astonishing military careers. The four wings on an already swift animal communicate the breathtaking speed of Alexander's conquests: he swept from Greece through Persia, Egypt, and into India in just over a decade. The four heads that follow speak of the division of his empire after his sudden death among his four generals — Lysimachus, Cassander, Seleucus, and Ptolemy — each taking a portion of the world Alexander had conquered.

# The Fourth Beast — Rome and the Antichrist (7:7-8)

The fourth beast is unlike anything in the natural world — dreadful, terrible, with iron teeth that devour and crush. This is Rome: the empire that destroyed Jerusalem in 70 AD, persecuted the early church, and dominated the known world for centuries. The ten horns represent the ten kingdoms that arose from Rome's dissolution. The little horn that rises and uproots three of the ten horns represents the antichrist — the man of sin who will make war with God's saints, overpower them, and speak blasphemous words against God.

This is the most sobering dimension of the vision: God's saints will be overpowered by the antichrist. The tribulation passages of Matthew 24 and 2 Timothy 3 are confirmed here — the last days will bring genuine, severe opposition to the people of God. But the vision does not end with the little horn's victory. It ends with the Ancient of Days seated in judgment and the beast thrown into the lake of fire.

# The Ancient of Days — The Court is Seated (7:9-12)

At the height of the beast's apparent power, Daniel's vision pivots to the heavenly court. The Ancient of Days takes His seat — His garment white as snow, His throne like a fiery flame. Millions of angels minister to Him. Tens of millions await judgment. The books are opened. The fourth beast is slain and its body destroyed and given to the burning flame. The other beasts have their dominion taken away, though their lives are prolonged for a season.

This heavenly scene is the interpretive anchor for everything else in the passage. The beasts are not ultimately in control of history — God is seated, the books are open, and the court is in session. Every act of the little horn, every war against the saints, every blasphemous word spoken against God — all of it is being recorded and will be adjudicated by the One who was Ancient before the first beast ever rose from the sea.

# The Son of Man — Kingdom Without End (7:13-14)

After the judgment of the beasts, Daniel sees one like the Son of Man coming with the clouds of heaven — approaching the Ancient of Days and receiving from Him dominion, glory, and a kingdom. All peoples, nations, and languages will serve Him. His dominion is an everlasting dominion that will not pass away and His kingdom is one that will not be destroyed. And the saints of the Most High will receive that kingdom and possess it forever — even forever and ever.

This is the destination toward which all of Daniel 7 is moving. The beasts rise, roar, and devour — but they are temporary. The kingdom of the Son of Man is eternal. The believer who holds this vision clearly does not despair at the power of the beast — they endure, because they know that the One who receives the kingdom has already overcome, and they will reign with Him.

## FURTHER APPLICATION

**1. Read history through Daniel's lens** — The rise and fall of empires is not random. It is the outworking of a prophetic programme that God revealed centuries in advance. Let this confidence in divine sovereignty shape how you interpret the news and the condition of the world.

**2. Expect the fourth beast's final form** — The antichrist is coming. The church must be theologically prepared for a season in which God's saints are overpowered temporarily. Do not build your faith on the assumption of earthly victory — build it on the certainty of eternal vindication.

**3. Keep the heavenly court in view** — When the power of earthly authority seems overwhelming, remember that the books are open, the Ancient of Days is seated, and every act of the beast is being recorded. Nothing is unaccountable. Nothing is outside the jurisdiction of heaven's court.

**4. Live as a citizen of the eternal kingdom** — The kingdom that the Son of Man receives is the kingdom you will inherit. Orient your daily choices, your investment of time and resources, and your relationships around the reality of a kingdom that will never be destroyed.

**5. Do not fear the beasts** — The most terrifying empire in history ends in the lake of fire. The most persecuted saints in history possess the kingdom forever. Fear is the wrong response to Daniel 7. Confidence in God's sovereign programme is the right one.
analysis_points:
Daniel's vision of four beasts is not mythology — it is a precise prophetic map of world empires from Babylon to the end of time.

The inner character of a kingdom matters more to God than its outward power — the beasts reveal the bestial nature of godless rule.

Every world empire that has risen has also fallen — the pattern of Daniel 7 is not cyclical but linear, moving toward a fixed divine conclusion.

The Ancient of Days is not a distant observer of history — He is seated, prepared, and ready to judge the world in its entirety.

The fourth beast is the most terrifying in history, but its end is the most certain — it will be thrown into hell.

The little horn that wars against God's saints is not ultimately victorious — when Christ comes, the saints possess the kingdom.

No matter how fierce the beast, the kingdom belongs to the saints of the Most High — forever, even forever and ever.

The antichrist will overpower God's people temporarily — but Christ's coming reverses every verdict the enemy has issued.

Daniel 7 is not primarily a lesson about world politics — it is a declaration about the certainty of God's kingdom over every human empire.

The believer who understands Daniel 7 does not fear the beasts of this age — they know how the story ends.

evening_notes: Cross References:  Psalm 118:8-9; Proverbs 29:25;  Isaiah 31:1; Psalm 146:3-5; Jeremiah 17:7-8; 2 Chronicles 32:8; Micah 5:10-11; Proverbs 3:5-6; Isaiah 2:22; Romans 8:6-8; Galatians 6:8; Philippians 3:3-4
analysis:
## BACKGROUND & CONTEXT

Matthew 24 is Jesus' most extended discourse on the end times — the Olivet Discourse — delivered to His disciples on the Mount of Olives just days before His crucifixion. The disciples had asked three questions: when will the Temple be destroyed, what will be the sign of His coming, and what will be the sign of the end of the age? Jesus answers all three, but the focus of this lesson falls on the Great Tribulation — the most severe period of the end times — and on what the believer is expected to do and know during it.

The lesson draws its summary from Acts 14 — the church-planting journey of Paul and Barnabas — and makes a connection that is both pastorally significant and theologically essential: the same apostles who planted churches also explicitly taught those churches that tribulation is the pathway, not the detour, to the kingdom. A church that has been taught to expect comfort as the norm of Christian life is a church that will collapse when the tribulation comes.

## SUMMARY & APPLICATION

# The Sacrilegious Object and the Signal to Run (Matthew 24:15-16)

Jesus references Daniel's prophecy of the abomination of desolation — the sacrilegious object that causes desecration set up in the holy place. This is the signal event that marks the beginning of the most severe phase of the Great Tribulation. When the disciples see this, Jesus' instruction is urgent and specific: run for the mountains. Do not go back for belongings. Do not delay. The instruction is not theological reflection — it is immediate, physical action.

This specificity is significant. Jesus does not give the disciples a general principle for enduring tribulation in this moment — He gives them a concrete, situational command. The implication is that the faithful watchman must know the times, read the signs, and be ready to act decisively when the moment of greatest danger arrives. Preparation for tribulation is not only spiritual — it is practical.

# The Elect and the Shortened Days (Matthew 24:16-22)

One of the most comforting details in Jesus' description of the Great Tribulation is verse 22: unless those days were shortened, no flesh would be saved. But for the elect's sake those days will be shortened. The severity of the tribulation is not in question — Jesus calls it a great tribulation such as has not been since the beginning of the world. But its duration is not left to the enemy's discretion. God Himself sets the limit. The elect are not immune from tribulation — but they are specifically factored into God's sovereign management of it.

This is the pastoral heart of the passage: the elect are not forgotten in the tribulation. They are the reason the days are shortened. Their presence in the tribulation changes its parameters. The believer who understands this does not enter tribulation as a victim of circumstances — they enter it as one whose welfare God has specifically calculated into the duration of the trial.

# Deception as the Primary Weapon of the Tribulation Period (Matthew 24:23-26)

Jesus' most repeated warning about the tribulation is not about physical danger — it is about deception. Then if anyone says to you, look, here is the Christ, or there — do not believe it. False christs and false prophets will arise and show great signs and wonders, so as to deceive, if possible, even the elect. The enemy's primary strategy in the tribulation is not violence alone — it is the manufacture of convincing counterfeits.

The subtlety described in verses 16-22 — what the elect are to do — is therefore not only physical relocation but spiritual alertness. The believer who has been formed on the original NT faith, who knows the Scriptures, who has been discipled in the patterns of genuine godliness, will be equipped to identify the counterfeit. The believer who has been raised on religious form without power will be among the most vulnerable to deception.

# The Cosmic Signs and the Coming King (Matthew 24:29)

After the tribulation of those days, the cosmic order itself participates in the announcement of Christ's return: the sun is darkened, the moon gives no light, the stars fall from the sky, and the powers of heaven are shaken. These are not incidental details of a natural disaster — they are the universe responding to the approaching King. The powers of heaven being shaken is not a cause for terror in the believer who has been watching and waiting — it is the confirmation that the kingdom of God is drawing near.

Luke 21:28 provides the believer's correct posture when these things begin to happen: look up and lift up your heads, because your redemption draws near. The signs that terrify the unbelieving world are the signals that the believing community has been waiting for.

# Paul, Barnabas, and the Theology of Tribulation (Acts 14:21-22)

The summary of this lesson draws from Acts 14 — Paul and Barnabas returning to the very cities where they had been persecuted to strengthen the disciples and exhort them to continue in the faith. Their message was not that the tribulation was over or that comfort was coming — it was that we must through many tribulations enter the kingdom of God. This was not a concession to difficult circumstances. It was a theological statement about the nature of the Christian journey.

They taught and practiced in their lives the principles of suffering for godly living. The disciples in Lystra, Iconium, and Antioch were not given a theology of tribulation from a safe distance — they were being taught by men who had just experienced it, who had returned to the same places where they were stoned and driven out, who embodied the very endurance they were calling the churches to embrace. This is the most credible form of discipleship in the area of suffering — not instruction from safety, but companionship in the fire.

## FURTHER APPLICATION

**1. Prepare for tribulation as a theological reality** — If your understanding of the Christian life does not include a robust theology of suffering and tribulation, you have been under-discipled. Return to Acts 14:22 and build your expectation on what Jesus and His apostles actually taught.

**2. Know the signs** — Jesus gave specific, detailed signs of the approaching tribulation. Study them, know them, and develop the spiritual alertness to read the times accurately so that when the moment of greatest urgency comes, you are not caught off guard.

**3. Guard against deception above all else** — The primary danger in the last days is not physical suffering but spiritual deception. Build your life on the original NT faith so thoroughly that the counterfeits do not find purchase in your heart.

**4. Teach suffering honestly** — If you are in any position of spiritual influence, do not disciple people into an expectation of comfort. Teach them Acts 14:22. Equip them for the tribulation pathway into the kingdom.

**5. Look up when the signs intensify** — Train yourself now to respond to increasing darkness with upward orientation rather than downward despair. The cosmic signs are not the end of hope — they are the announcement of the King.
analysis_points:
Tribulation is not an aberration of the Christian life — it is the announced pathway into the kingdom of God.

The Great Tribulation is not merely a future event to be survived — it is a present reality to be navigated with faith and endurance.

Deception intensifies in the last days — many will claim to be Christ, and the elect must be prepared to recognise the counterfeit.

The elect are not promised immunity from tribulation — they are promised that the days will be shortened for their sake.

Suffering does not disqualify the believer — it is the school in which the principles of godly living are most deeply learned.

Paul and Barnabas taught not only doctrine but the necessity of suffering — a church that is unprepared for tribulation is a church that has been poorly discipled.

The wrath of God and the subtlety of the enemy operate simultaneously in the tribulation period — the believer must be alert to both.

Those who hear and obey the gospel establish themselves as the church that will endure through the most severe part of the Great Tribulation.

Christians must be taught that suffering is not a sign of God's absence — it is the hallway through which the eternal kingdom is entered.

The powers of heaven being shaken is not a cause for panic in the believer — it is the signal that the kingdom of God is drawing near.

## LESSON GUIDELINES

Paul warns of the great apostasy (2 Timothy 3).

# 1. The Perversions (3:1-9)

## a. The Evil (3:1-5)

** i. ** People will love only themselves and their money (2 Timothy 3:1-2a)

** ii. ** They will be proud, abusive, disobedient to their parents, ungrateful, and unholy (3:2b)

** iii. ** They will be without love, unforgiving, slanderous, without self-control, and brutal (3:3)

** iv. ** They will be treacherous and will be lovers of pleasure rather than lovers of God (3:4)

** v. ** They will have a form of godliness but will deny its power (3:5)

## Summary

The last days of salvation history began at Pentecost and will be concluded with the second coming of Christ. Paul prophesies through the Holy Spirit that evil in the world will accelerate and intensify as the end approaches.

1. As the conclusion of the last days approaches, there will be a widespread collapse of the moral structure of the family and of society in general as people are arrogant "lovers of pleasures more than lovers of God." These times will be especially grievous and trying for God's true servants.

2. Paul issues the warning that within organized Christianity, many will have "a form of godliness", i.e., hypocritical religion, but will deny the power of the gospel that produces genuine godliness. Paul adds, "from such turn away." The full blessing of salvation in Christ Jesus and the mighty end-time outpouring of the Holy Spirit will occur in and through the church that has passion for Jesus, longs for His coming as the Bridegroom and carries the fire of God in true NT faith and ministry. There will be even greater grace and power for those believers and churches who hold fast to the original faith entrusted to the saints.

References: 1 Timothy 4:1; Acts 2:17; Jude 17:18; 2 Peter 3:3; Acts 3:3; Romans 5:20; Jude 3; 1 John 2:18.
discussion_questions:
Paul says the last days began at Pentecost — how does this understanding change the way we relate to the signs of the times we observe around us today?

Why does Paul identify self-love and love of money as the twin roots of last-days evil — how do these two orientations produce all the other perversions he lists?

The collapse of family relationships — son against father, daughter against mother — is listed among the signs of the last days. In what ways is this visible in contemporary society, and how should the church respond?

What is the difference between a form of godliness and genuine godliness — and how does a believer test which one they are living?

Paul says "from such turn away" regarding those who have a form of godliness without power — how does a believer apply this instruction without becoming isolated or judgmental?

How does the promise of greater grace and power for those who hold fast to original NT faith reframe the believer's experience of last-days pressure and difficulty?

Jesus compares the last days to the days of Noah — not because people were visibly wicked, but because they were absorbed in ordinary life without watching. What does this say about the specific danger of comfort and normalcy for the last-days believer?

Paul's experience in 2 Corinthians 1 describes suffering as producing patient endurance and becoming a resource to help others — how does this connect to the last-days context of 2 Timothy 3?

What does it look like practically for a church to carry the fire of God in true NT faith and ministry in the last days — and what would need to change in most churches to move in that direction?

If evil is intensifying as the end approaches, and grace is also intensifying for those who hold fast — what specific choices position a believer to be in the stream of increasing grace rather than increasing corruption?
evening_title: THE BLESSING OF THE FAITHFUL ONE
evening_notes: Cross References: Matthew 25:21-23; 1 Corinthians 1-2; Matthew 24:45-47; Revelation 2:10; Luke 16:10-12; 1 Corinthians 4:2; Proverbs 28:20; Daniel 12:3; Hebrews 11:6; Romans 2:7; Matthew 25:23; 2 Timothy 4:8
analysis:
## BACKGROUND & CONTEXT

2 Timothy 3 is one of the most forensically accurate passages in all of Scripture when measured against the observable condition of contemporary society. Paul writes this letter from a Roman prison — his final letter before his execution — and he uses it to prepare Timothy, and through him the church, for what the last days will look like. His prophecy is not vague or symbolic. It is a precise, itemised list of character traits that will define the people of the last days. The list is so comprehensive, and so recognisable, that it serves as both a warning and a compass — helping the believer identify the spirit of the age and resist being shaped by it.

## SUMMARY & APPLICATION

# The Days We Are Living In (2 Timothy 3:1)

Paul opens with a declaration that frames everything that follows: know this, that in the last days perilous times will come. The word "perilous" carries the sense of something fierce, dangerous, and difficult to endure — the same word used in Matthew 8:28 to describe the two demon-possessed men who were so violent no one could pass that way. Paul is saying that the last days will produce a society that is spiritually and morally violent — dangerous to navigate, grievous to live through, and especially trying for those who are committed to genuine godliness.

Crucially, the last days did not begin at some point in the distant future — they began at Pentecost. The church has been living in the last days since the outpouring of the Spirit in Acts 2. What changes as the end approaches is the intensity. Evil accelerates. The perversions deepen. The contrast between the genuine church and the cultural religion of the age becomes sharper.

# The Root — Self-Love and Love of Money (2 Timothy 3:1-2a)

Paul traces every specific manifestation of last-days evil back to two roots: people will love only themselves and their money. These are not peripheral sins — they are foundational orientations. Self-love replaces the love of God as the organising principle of life. Love of money replaces the love of neighbour. When these two loves dominate a society, every other institution — family, community, church, government — is eventually corrupted by them. The long list of character traits that follows in verses 2-5 is not a random catalogue. It is a description of what self-love and materialism produce when given a full generation to work.

# The Catalogue — What the Last Days Look Like (2 Timothy 3:2-5)

Paul's list is exhaustive in its coverage and uncomfortable in its recognisability: proud, abusive, disobedient to parents, ungrateful, unholy, without natural affection, unforgiving, slanderous, without self-control, brutal, despisers of good, treacherous, reckless, conceited, lovers of pleasure more than lovers of God. This is not a description of the openly wicked — it is a description of people who have a form of godliness. These traits are appearing inside organised religion, not just outside it.

The collapse of the family described in the memory verse — son against father, daughter against mother, a man's enemies being those of his own household — is not incidental to this list. It is its domestic expression. When self-love is the governing principle of a society, the family, which requires self-sacrifice to function, is the first casualty.

# The Most Dangerous Verse — A Form of Godliness (2 Timothy 3:5)

The climax of Paul's description is verse 5: having a form of godliness but denying its power. This is the most dangerous category in the entire list — not because it is the most visibly wicked, but because it is the hardest to detect and the easiest to inhabit. A form of godliness looks like genuine faith. It uses the right language, attends the right services, and performs the right rituals. But it has been emptied of the transforming power of the Holy Spirit. It produces no genuine repentance, no authentic love, no real holiness, and no fire.

Paul's instruction regarding this category is direct and non-negotiable: from such turn away. This is not a call to gentle critique or careful dialogue. It is a call to separation. The believer who remains in an environment of religious form without spiritual power will eventually be shaped by it. The antidote is to hold fast to the original faith entrusted to the saints — the NT apostolic gospel in its full, unedited power.

# The Promise for the Genuine Church

The summary holds one extraordinary promise in the middle of its catalogue of last-days horrors: there will be even greater grace and power for those believers and churches who hold fast to the original faith. As darkness intensifies, the light of the genuine church does not diminish — it becomes more visible by contrast. The end-time outpouring of the Holy Spirit is not for the church that has made peace with the spirit of the age. It is for the church that has passion for Jesus, longs for His coming, and carries the fire of God in true NT faith and ministry. Romans 5:20 is the assurance: where sin abounded, grace abounded much more.

# The Coming That Changes Everything (Matthew 24:37-44)

The second coming of Christ is the fixed horizon against which all last-days living must be oriented. Jesus' comparison to the days of Noah is precise: people were eating, drinking, marrying, and giving in marriage — not doing obviously wicked things, but living as though this world was the only world and this moment was the only moment. Then the flood came. The lesson for the last-days believer is equally precise: watch, be ready, and do not be caught living as though He is not coming.

## FURTHER APPLICATION

**1. Know the times** — The conditions Paul describes are not future — they are present. Develop the ability to identify the spirit of the age so that you can resist being unconsciously shaped by it.

**2. Guard against self-love** — Audit honestly where self-interest has been overriding love for God and neighbour in your daily decisions. The root must be dealt with before the fruit can be changed.

**3. Turn away from religious form without power** — If the environment you are in has the language of godliness but none of its transforming power, take Paul's instruction seriously: from such turn away.

**4. Hold fast to the original faith** — The NT apostolic gospel is not a starting point to be graduated from. It is the foundation to be returned to, re-examined, and held with increasing conviction as the last days intensify.

**5. Live with the second coming in view** — Let the certainty of Christ's return function as a daily orienting reality. Ask regularly: if He came today, would He find me watching and ready?
analysis_points:
The last days did not begin at some distant future point — they began at Pentecost and are intensifying as the end approaches.

Every moral collapse visible in society today was prophesied centuries ago — the believer should be sobered, not surprised.

A form of godliness without its power is not a lesser version of Christianity — it is a counterfeit that must be turned away from.

Self-love and love of money are the twin roots from which every other social evil in the last days grows.

The family is the first institution to collapse when a society abandons God — the memory verse is not a metaphor, it is a forecast.

Evil in the last days will not only be external to the church — it will infiltrate organized Christianity under the cover of religious language.

The believer who holds fast to original NT faith will experience greater grace and power, not less, as darkness intensifies.

Suffering and patient endurance are not signs that God has abandoned the last-days believer — they are the marks of authentic faith in a collapsing world.

The second coming of Christ is the fixed point on which all last-days expectation is anchored — it will come suddenly and without warning.

Passion for Jesus, longing for His coming, and carrying the fire of God in true NT faith and ministry are the distinguishing marks of the genuine last-days church.

title: THE DUTY OF FAITHFUL WATCHMAN OR PASTOR

body:
## LESSON GUIDELINES

Ezekiel uses various images to depict Israel's relationship with her leaders.

# 1. The Watchman and the Wall (33:1-33)

## a. God and the Messengers to Israel (33:1-9)

Here a distinction is made between a faithful watchman and an unfaithful watchman or messenger.

# i. The Faithful Watchman (33:1-5, 7, 9)

This kind of prophet — like Ezekiel — keeps on warning the people to repent even if they refuse to listen.

# ii. The Faithless Watchman (33:6, 8)

The blood of the guilty is on his hands for not warning the people.

## b. The Role (3:15-21)

Ezekiel assumes the role of a spiritual watchman by delivering a twofold warning.

# i. To the Godless (3:16-19)

Cease your wicked ways, or die.

# ii. To the Godly (3:20-21)

Continue your good ways, or die.

## c. The Restriction (3:22-27)

Ezekiel is to imprison himself in his own house, where God will temporarily cause him to be unable to speak.

## SUMMARY

The watchman who saw destruction coming and did not warn the people would be held responsible for their blood.

1. Likewise in the kingdom of God, a prophet or preacher who does not warn a lukewarm church of coming judgment will be held responsible for the people's blood.

2. To a great extent all believers have the responsibility to witness to the lost and to help fulfill the mission task given to the church by Jesus. We will have to give an account to God if we refuse to obey Jesus' Great Commission.

#REFERENCES:
 *Matthew 28:19; Acts 20:26; Jeremiah 3:15; Ezekiel 34:23-24; Ephesians 4:11; Acts 20:28.*
discussion_questions:
Why does God frame the prophet's responsibility through the image of a watchman rather than a teacher or a priest — what does the military analogy add to our understanding of the calling?

The faithful watchman warns even when people refuse to listen — what does this say about the relationship between faithfulness and outcomes in ministry?

 In what specific ways does modern church culture create pressure on spiritual leaders to silence or soften the warning — and how should a faithful watchman respond to that pressure?

What does it mean that the blood of the unwarned falls on the watchman's hands — and how should this reality shape the way every believer engages with the people around them?

Why does Ezekiel's commission include a warning to the righteous as well as the godless — what dangerous assumption does this challenge?

The restriction of Ezekiel — God silencing him as a message to the people — what does this teach about what happens when a people persistently refuses to hear?

How does the Great Commission connect to the watchman's calling — in what sense is every believer a watchman in their own sphere?

Paul declared himself innocent of all men's blood because he had preached the whole counsel of God — what portions of the whole counsel are most commonly omitted in contemporary preaching, and why?

 What is the difference between a prophet who is silent because God has restricted him and a prophet who is silent because he is afraid — and how does a leader know which one they are?

 If you were to give an account today of everyone in your life who needed a warning and received one from you — how would that account look?

## SECTION B — DETAILED ANALYSIS

## BACKGROUND & CONTEXT

Ezekiel 33 is a pivotal chapter in the book — it stands at the midpoint between Ezekiel's oracles of judgment against Israel and his oracles of restoration. God gives Ezekiel a new commission, framed through one of Scripture's most vivid analogies: the watchman on the wall. The watchman's role in the ancient world was simple and critical — he stood at the highest point of the city and scanned the horizon. If he saw an enemy approaching, he blew the trumpet. If he stayed silent, he was not merely negligent — he was criminally responsible for every life lost in the attack he failed to announce.

God applies this image directly to Ezekiel — and by extension to every spiritual leader and believer entrusted with the knowledge of God's truth. The analogy is deliberately uncomfortable. It removes the escape route of silence. It closes the door on the idea that keeping quiet is a neutral option. In the kingdom of God, a watchman who sees and stays silent has made a deadly choice.

## SUMMARY & APPLICATION

# The Faithful Watchman — Warning as Worship (Ezekiel 33:1-5, 7, 9)

The faithful watchman is not defined by his popularity or by the response he receives. He is defined by one thing: he warns. Even when the people cover their ears, even when the message is unwelcome, even when the culture around him insists that prophets should be positive and encouraging — he warns. Ezekiel is explicitly told: whether they hear or whether they refuse, they will know that a prophet has been among them.

This is one of the most liberating truths in pastoral ministry — and one of the most challenging. The faithful minister is not responsible for the response. He is responsible for the message. If the warning is given and the people refuse to hear, their blood is on their own heads. But if the warning is withheld, the blood falls on the watchman. The criterion is not success. It is faithfulness.

Isaiah 58:1 — the memory verse of this lesson — captures the nature of this faithfulness with precision: cry aloud, spare not, lift up your voice like a trumpet. The word "spare not" is the critical phrase. Do not soften. Do not qualify. Do not dilute the message to make it more palatable. Lift your voice like a trumpet — clear, piercing, and unmistakable.

# The Faithless Watchman — Silence as Blood Guilt (Ezekiel 33:6, 8)

The faithless watchman is not necessarily a wicked man. He may simply be a conflict-averse man — one who has calculated that the cost of warning is higher than the cost of silence. He sees the sword coming. He knows what is approaching. But he says nothing. And God's verdict is devastating: his blood I will require at the watchman's hand.

This is perhaps the most sobering statement in the entire passage for anyone in spiritual leadership. The people who perish under judgment having never been warned — their blood is credited to the account of the leader who knew and said nothing. Ministry that prioritises the comfort of the congregation over the truth of the Word is not pastoral — it is a form of spiritual negligence that carries eternal consequences.

The modern church faces this temptation in acute form. A culture that increasingly treats personal preference as the highest authority, and discomfort as a form of harm, creates enormous pressure on spiritual leaders to edit, soften, and manage God's message. Ezekiel 33 offers no concession to this pressure. The watchman's job is to warn. Everything else — reception, response, relationship — comes after that.

# The Twofold Warning — To the Godless and the Godly (Ezekiel 3:16-21)

Ezekiel's commission was not only to the wicked. It was equally to the righteous. To the godless: cease your wicked ways or die — the offer of repentance is still open, but the path of wickedness leads to destruction. To the godly: continue your good ways or die — the righteous person who turns from righteousness has no immunity from judgment on the basis of their past obedience.

This twofold warning is theologically significant. It dismantles two equally dangerous errors: the error of the wicked who think they are beyond reach, and the error of the righteous who think their previous faithfulness makes them safe regardless of their present condition. No one is beyond warning. No one is beyond the need for it.

# The Restriction — When God Silences the Watchman (Ezekiel 3:22-27)

One of the most unusual aspects of Ezekiel's commission is the restriction: God tells him to imprison himself in his own house and temporarily silences him — making him unable to speak except when God opens his mouth. This period of enforced silence was not punishment — it was itself a message. A people who had consistently refused to hear God's word would experience the withdrawal of it. The silence of the prophet communicated what the words had failed to communicate: you are in a moment of divine restraint, and you should take it seriously.

This dimension of the passage challenges every believer to take seriously the privilege of having access to God's word and God's messengers. The silence that follows persistent rejection is not neutral — it is judicial.

# Every Believer is a Watchman

The summary of this lesson extends the watchman's responsibility beyond the ordained ministry to every believer. To a great extent all believers have the responsibility to witness to the lost. The Great Commission of Matthew 28:19 was not issued to apostles alone — it was issued to disciples. Every person who has received the gospel carries the responsibility of the watchman in their own sphere of influence. We will have to give an account to God if we refuse to obey.

Acts 20:26-27 records Paul's own testimony of watchman faithfulness: I am innocent of the blood of all men, for I have not shunned to declare to you the whole counsel of God. That is the standard. The whole counsel. Not the comfortable portions. Not the popular themes. The whole counsel — including judgment, repentance, accountability, and the cost of discipleship.

## FURTHER APPLICATION

**1. Examine what you are not saying** — The faithful watchman is judged not only by what he preaches but by what he withholds. Is there a message you have been softening, qualifying, or avoiding? Name it and preach it.

**2. Separate faithfulness from fruitfulness** — Your responsibility before God is to warn, not to guarantee results. Release the burden of response and carry only the burden of faithfulness.

**3. Warn the righteous as well as the wicked** — Do not assume that the spiritually mature in your care are beyond the need for warning. Ezekiel's commission was twofold — both audiences needed to hear.

**4. Take the Great Commission personally** — Matthew 28:19 was issued to you. Your workplace, your neighbourhood, your family, your sphere of daily life — these are your wall to watch. Who in your life is approaching destruction without knowing it?

**5. Give account before you are asked to** — Acts 20:26 shows Paul accounting for his faithfulness while he still had the opportunity. Do not wait for judgment to reveal what could be corrected now.
analysis_points:
A watchman who sees destruction coming and stays silent has not been merciful — he has been complicit.

The blood of the unwarned is on the hands of the watchman who knew and said nothing.

Faithfulness in ministry is measured not by the response of the people but by the consistency of the warning.

The faithful watchman warns even when the people refuse to listen — his responsibility ends at the warning, not at the response.

God's word to the godless and the godly carries equal weight — both must hear, and the watchman must deliver both messages.

A prophet or preacher who softens the message to avoid offence has already begun to fail his calling.

Every believer shares in the responsibility to witness — the Great Commission is not reserved for ordained ministers.

Silence in the face of sin is not neutrality — it is a choice with eternal consequences for those left unwarned.

The watchman's restriction — being silenced by God — was itself a form of divine message to a people who had refused to hear.

We will give account to God for every soul we could have reached and did not.

## LESSON GUIDELINES

## HIS PRIVATE MINISTRY IN GAZA (Acts 8:26-40)

# 1. His Message from an Angel (8:26)

Philip is instructed to go to the Gaza desert.

# 2. His Meeting with a Eunuch (8:27-40)

## a. The Charge Given to the Eunuch (8:27)

Candace, Queen of Ethiopia, has entrusted all her riches to him.

## b. The Confusion of the Eunuch (8:28-34)

Philip finds this man reading from the scriptures.

# i. The Passage (8:28)

He is reading from Isaiah 53:7-8 and cannot understand what he is reading.

# ii. The Problem (8:29-34)

The Eunuch asks Philip if the prophet is speaking of himself or someone else.

## c. The Clarification to the Eunuch (8:35)

Philip preaches the gospel to him.

## d. The Conversation of the Eunuch (8:36-37)

He confesses that Jesus Christ is the Son of God, and Philip baptizes him.

# 3. His Ministry at Azotus (8:36-40)

After the Eunuch is baptized, the Holy Spirit immediately catches Philip away and brings him to the city of Azotus, where Philip resumes his teaching and he travels to Caesarea.

## SUMMARY

In obedience to the Spirit, Philip ran to the chariot of the Eunuch. He did not approach the Eunuch with an arrogant attitude. He simply asked a question to begin a discussion concerning the Bible. The Eunuch was confused concerning the interpretation of Isaiah 53 which he was reading. The Jewish teachers in Jerusalem had said that Isaiah prophesied about himself. However, in Jerusalem the Christians, whom the Eunuch had surely encountered in the temple courtyard, affirmed that Isaiah was talking about the crucified Messiah they identified as Jesus. In any case, the Eunuch realized that he needed further instruction.

The Eunuch was reading Isaiah 53:7-8 which was a prophecy that Jesus would be led to crucifixion as an innocent sheep is led to slaughter and an unknowing lamb to the shearer. Jesus, in His humiliation as the Son of God, submitted to the cross because He knew that it was for the salvation of man. The Eunuch was confused as to whether this passage was speaking of Isaiah as the Jewish Rabbis taught, or if it was a prophecy of Jesus as the Christians in Jerusalem affirmed. Philip then took this opportunity to complete the Eunuch's knowledge of Jesus. Jesus was the subject of Philip's preaching. It is God's system of evangelism to use preachers and teachers of the word of God in order to communicate the gospel (Romans 10:14-15). After Philip had declared the death, burial and resurrection of Jesus, the Eunuch realized that according to Philip's instructions, he must obey this good news by immersion in water for the remission of his sins.

**References: Isaiah 53:7-8; Matthew 10.**
discussion_questions:
Why do you think God sent Philip to a desert road rather than to a more populated location — what does this say about where divine appointments happen?

Philip ran to the chariot when the Spirit spoke — what does this immediate obedience reveal about the relationship between sensitivity to the Spirit and effective evangelism?

What made Philip's opening question — "do you understand what you are reading?" — so effective, and how can believers apply this approach in everyday conversations?

The Eunuch was already in the Scriptures but needed someone to explain them — what does this say about the role of the church in helping people who are already seeking?

Why is it significant that Philip preached Jesus specifically from Isaiah 53 — and what does this model teach us about how to present the gospel from any Scripture?

Romans 10:14-15 says the gospel travels through people — how does this passage challenge the idea that evangelism is the responsibility of professional ministers alone?

The Eunuch asked for baptism immediately after believing — what does this urgency reveal about the nature of genuine faith, and what can the church learn from it?

After Philip was caught away, the Eunuch went on his way rejoicing without a mentor, a church, or a follow-up programme — what does this say about the sufficiency of the gospel and the Holy Spirit?

In what ways does the story of Philip and the Eunuch challenge the typical conditions we set before we consider ourselves ready to evangelise?

 If God needed Philip for a single encounter on a desert road, what specific encounter might He be positioning you for right now — and are you available?
